Question: How often are state voter rolls purged of non-citizens or updated of voters citizenship changes?
Answer: To answer the specific question here: States don’t clean up records very often — it costs too much money. They only do it when it of political advantage. Updating citizen status (i. e. corrections and naturalizations) is almost never done unless a voter takes the initiative. I have professional expertise in statewide database matching. There are some resources that states can draw on to help keep the voter rolls up do date. These three paths all share the same problems. The first is the accuracy of data, which could include clerical errors. The second is record matching errors between databases, which is a big deal. And the final one is the currency of data. Some 875,000 non-citizens are naturalized each year. DMV data becomes instantly stale the moment is entered. SAVE data is not necessarily correct or up to date. Unless the newly naturalized citizen takes action to notify SSA, they will not know. So after identifying a potential non-citizen, a state has two options: There is a nationwide electronic system called EVVE (Electronic Verification of Vital Events)[2] that many states use for their DMV to validate birth records. That system could reasonably be used to verify persons who are born in the United States and of course DMVs who use EVVE could note in their database that they had a verified citizen. The number of non-citizen voters prosecuted for that crime is tiny, leading me to believe that the states who rail about a huge problem are only guessing. Clearing up the voter registration database the right way requires a state to actually want to solve the problem rather than having a political talking point. It’s totally doable, but it requires competence, cooperation and manpower.
